title: Roham Gharegozlou | The Past, Present, and Future of Crypto | Talks at Google
description:
Roham Gharegozlou discusses his company Dapper Labs, the detailed history of cryptocurrency and where he sees it going in the near future.

Roham Gharegozlou is the co-founder and CEO of Dapper Labs and a leader in blockchain and Web3 technology. He is often cited as the pioneer of NFTs, with CryptoKitties being the first viral NFT project that broke Ethereum in 2017. From those learnings, Roham launched Dapper Labs from Axiom Zen in 2018, aiming to drive mainstream adoption of decentralized technologies and put a crypto wallet in every pocket. Today, Dapper Labs has made Web3 accessible for developers, creators, and users by designing Flow, a decentralized Web3 platform built for consumer-friendly dApps that now has more than 3.6 million accounts; releasing Dapper Wallet, the easiest way to get started on Web3; and launching dApps, including NBA Top Shot (with more than 1.3M community members and nearly $1B in sales), UFC Strike, NFL ALL DAY, Seussibles, and more that are attracting millions to Web3.

For more information on Dapper Labs, please visit https://www.dapperlabs.com/.

Moderated by David Lawee.

David Lawee founded CapitalG, Alphabet's independent growth fund, in 2013, drawing on his experience at Google and as a serial entrepreneur. Since then, he has helped transform high-potential startups into some of the most highly-valued businesses of our generation, including Airbnb, Lyft, Snap, Robinhood, Credit Karma, Niantic, Digital Currency Group, and Fireblocks. Previously, David played a pivotal role in Google’s growth story, first as Google’s CMO and then as the company’s first VP of corporate development where his team led more than 100 acquisitions for the company. Before joining Google, David successfully founded a number of startup ventures including Xfire, a leading online gaming community acquired by Viacom, and Mosaic Venture Partners, a Toronto-based venture capital firm.

For more information on CapitalG please visit https://capitalg.com/.

summary: The speaker argues that major technology companies like Google, Netflix, Amazon, and Microsoft are relevant to the crypto ecosystem but currently lack a clear role in legitimizing it. He suggests that Google Cloud could serve as a significant infrastructure partner for the Flow platform, while noting that even large, stable assets like Netflix are not immune to market volatility similar to Bitcoin. Ultimately, the talk posits that these tech giants have the potential to help legitimize the crypto space, though their current involvement is questioned or undefined.

transcript: [MUSIC PLAYING] DAVID LAWEE: I'm incredibly excited to introduce Roham to discuss his company, Dapper Labs, the history of NFTs, and where he sees his company and the space going in the future. I'll give a brief introduction of Roham. And then we'll have a conversation for about 40 minutes and then give the audience time to ask questions for the last 20 minutes. Roham is by all accounts, in every way, a leader in the blockchain and Web3 technology community and was really the pioneer of NFTs, or at least their kind of first wave of NFTs with "CryptoKitties," which was a viral product that broke out in 2017 and practically broke Ethereum for some time. From those learnings, Roham launched Dapper Labs with a mission to drive mainstream adoption, and decentralize technologies, and put a crypto wallet in every pocket. Today, Dapper Labs has made Web3 accessible for developers, creators, and users by designing the Flow ecosystem, a decentralized Web3 platform which has really distinguished itself by being consumer-friendly and has the-- the platform has more than 3.6 million accounts. And the games include NBA Top Shot, which has 1.3 million members and has had over $1 billion in sales, UFC Strike, NFL All Day, Seussibles, and a number of others. The company has raised $650 million and most recently was valued at $7.6 billion. Before founding Axiom Zen, Roham served with Rising Tide fund in Silicon Valley as a partner focused on seed stage investments. And he holds a BA and an MS degree in economics and biological sciences from Stanford University. And with that, welcome, Roham. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Thank you. Thanks for having me. DAVID LAWEE: I thought we would kick things off just giving you a chance to give the listeners a sense for the evolution of the business, starting with Axiom Zen, and the launch of "CryptoKitties," and what you learned from that. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Yeah, I mean, you gave a quick background. But I can give some of the details in the middle where we started working on-- I mean, the first time, at Axiom Zen, we tried building on blockchain was way back in 2014 with Bitcoin. But by 2017, we were super interested in non-currency applications of the technology and just looking at-- everything we wanted to build, we realized there was a key primitive missing, which is this concept of a non-fungible token, the ability to represent something that is individually unique, but part of a broader set. So that was why we started working on the non-fungible token standard in early summer 2017, published it by September 20, 2017, and then, a couple of months later, launched "CryptoKitties." To your point, it went viral immediately. It sort of was a financial success. We made millions of dollars in revenue very quickly. But it was also kind of a technological failure in the sense that it became impossible to play very quickly out the gate, both in terms of cost as well as reliability and other things on the Ethereum network. But it kickstarted the start of Dapper Labs. And since then, we sort of dedicated ourselves to saying, this technology can really help the mainstream. There's a big gap in terms of user experience, safety, the kinds of applications that add value to everyday people's lives rather than just being about speculation games and things like that. And so we started the journey, raised capital from some of the world's best folks, including your colleagues at Google Ventures, and have been sort of plugging away-- plugging away ever since. It's actually-- I just looked it up. We're over 10 million accounts on Flow. So it's been a cool few months where there's-- and we-- as Dapper Labs, we're two out of the five top five apps. But we're actually not the top two-- or Top Shot might be back at number two now. But there are other companies that are building products that are sort of coming strong out the gate and building a strong foundation, which I get super excited about. DAVID LAWEE: Awesome. How long did it take to come out with Flow? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Flow? So when we started the company-- so if you think about "CryptoKitties," November 28, we were working in the Ethereum ecosystem for a year and a half or more past that. And we tried building-- so we built the first smart contract wallet that was for consumers, first wallet to do pay for gas on user's behalf, first wallet to do key recovery, first wallet to integrate credit card payments into the flow. And we didn't give up on Ethereum until May 2019, when we had signed the deal with MBA. And we were just-- we couldn't credibly look at ourselves in the mirror and say we're going to bet the company's future on a technology we don't think is going to get there. We spend a lot of time with Vitalik and a lot of the developers behind other layer 1s. And along the way, we were sort of designing our perfect system. As app developers, what would be the platform that we would want to build on? And we were validating that with folks at Andreessen, Dan Bennett at Stanford, who later became a partner at Andreessen. He's an advisor to the company. Taher Elgamal at Salesforce, key inventor of SSL, he's an advisor to the company. So they helped validate that, hey, the approach we've taken and the things we want as developers make sense. And the approach we've taken is sound. And so May 2019 is when we started building Flow in earnest. Launched it in early alpha May 2020 with NBA Top Shot in early alpha and then came out of-- came into public beta October 2020. So it's taken a while. And even today, in about 15 days, Flow will become completely permissionless where any developer will be able to publish any piece of code to the network. And so that's taken a year and a half, two years of hardening, and scaling, and security work as well. So it's been quite an involved process. But the whole way, we felt really good, because we're dogfooding our own product. And Flow-- NBA Top Shot alone has more transactions than most other NFT projects combined. DAVID LAWEE: So when you first pitched the NBA, it was-- you didn't talk so much about which ecosystem you were going to build on? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: No, it wasn't immediately clear. Our goal as a company was mainstream adoption. It wasn't creating another layer 1 platform. And we wanted to be sure that it's something that necessitated it. It was contemplated within the agreement, but the default assumption was that someone else would figure something out. And then that never ended up happening. DAVID LAWEE: When did you first start talking to the NBA? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: March of 2018-- April 2018 [INAUDIBLE]. DAVID LAWEE: How long did it take to get to an agreement with them? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: A little over a year. DAVID LAWEE: OK, so they were pretty forward-thinking though, huh? Because I guess they were really-- after "CryptoKitties," there really weren't any significant projects while your discussions were going on. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Yeah, crypto winter set in pretty quick after "CryptoKitties" launched. And we were one of the few-- it was us, OpenSea, Sky Mavis, which is the "Axie Infinity" guys, and folks like Alchemy. And there was a very small subset of companies that were born in that flurry of activity and then sort of survived through the rest of the period. And not only was the NBA forward-thinking in the sense of working with us, but they were-- or sort of being open to working with us-- but they had a full team staff that whole year trying to really understand, hey, what's the regulatory framework that these assets are going to fall in? All our lawyers are telling us no. Let's deeply understand why and what position we're going to take. Because no one else has, right? There was no other-- other than-- "CryptoKitties" was sort of the best example, and that was from a startup. And so there was no other big brand that had taken that step. And so we spend a lot of time with them. I mean, our-- but we did that even before "CryptoKitties," where we were the first company to go to the securities regulators in Canada and sit down with them, explain to them what blockchain was, what smart contracts were, what NFTs-- this new thing called NFTs were. And they wrote their first no action letter in crypto about NFTs and said, hey, this is not a security. So we had some experience explaining this stuff to folks. But I think it was a necessary process. And I think getting the NBA was a necessary catalyst for just adoption of the whole space in general because it made it safe for a lot of other content owners and creators to participate in and made them realize, hey, this technology actually helps us protect our rights and create alignment with our customers rather than something that we should be scared of. DAVID LAWEE: Awesome. And so who thinks through the kind of tokenomics aspect of the game, like how many to launch of each shot, all of those types of nuances? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: I mean right now, there's a full-- there's sort of two layers. There's an economy team and a game design team. Originally, it was just one person that was sort of doing everything in their heads. And for "CryptoKitties," it was Dieter, my CTO. And so it kind of evolved from there. But each IP-- we have NBA, we have NFL, UFC-- has an economist as well as a game designer. The role of-- in a traditional game, the game designer owns the economy. But in a sort of open economy game, we want someone to also sort of be observing the macro movements and correlations between other economies. So it's split that way. And they use both data as well as instinct. And now they have new tools at their disposal. So we have both the ability to create new content as well as pull content out of the ecosystem. And so they kind of make those choices based on the customer experience they want to create. Our customers all do it differently. And I should mention NFTs are-- you can use them in a sort of game environment similar-- that's more live operated like NBA Top Shot. Or they can be an artist coming in from the street, taking a picture with an iPhone, minting 1,000 things just because they feel like it, pricing at $1 just because they feel like it, or putting an auction on it, whatever it may be. So it will look a lot more like social media, where it will be chaotic to an extent. Some post will go viral, some won't. Some things will be successful, some won't. There'll be a long tail of creators that no one cares about and creators that go viral quickly but then die out. It will be more dynamic. And I think our ecosystem is designed to handle both sides of it. But NBA Top Shot is a little more live operated like a game, where there's an economist, a game designer to look at the data. They make choices that are long-term-oriented. But it doesn't all have to be that way. Just like lots of social media accounts are very well-thought-out, lots of them are very organic and sort of impromptu. DAVID LAWEE: Awesome. So give me a sense for the distribution of [INAUDIBLE] across your company between some of these first-party games, the ecosystem development, and maybe kind of other things that you're doing. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Yeah, we're about a third sports studio. We're about a 40% studio, 60% platform. So a third sports studio is almost all. Almost everything that we do in first-party development is in the sports arena. We do some experimentation with "CryptoKitties" and others But even that is designed to say, how can we be-- create a seed that, then, others can build on? Because that's, in large part, what we think is special about Web3 is even an asset can be a platform, much less sort of an application. Every application is a platform, but every asset can also be a platform. So that's sort of the lens we take. We spend most of our first-party efforts on sports because we think we've-- there's a 1,000x opportunity right there. We've served a million NBA fans. There's a billion NBA fans. And so there's sort of immense opportunity there. On the platform side, our efforts are split between the core Flow open source development and then the sort of Dapper layer on top of that, which is payments, user experience, keep the assets safe, help the user discover their next product. It's the wallet layer. And our efforts there is probably also 60/40, with 60% on the wallet layer, 40% on the core blockchain. And the core blockchain effort has been going down over time as it becomes much more decentralized as others start contributing to the code base and taking over parts of it. There's a Flow Foundation now that is taking over parts of actually keeping the network running, and making economic decisions, and things like that. So it's [INAUDIBLE]. So the biggest chunk of our effort is our own first-party content. That's driving users and really demonstrating the power of the platform, which is not just the blockchain, but it's also that user experience layer on top of it. DAVID LAWEE: Awesome. Maybe give us a sense for what were the primary design principles of Flow, what you are trying to enable creators to do, and kind of how you see it evolving. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Yeah, I mean, I can get into some of the specifics. But I'll relay one conversation I had with Vitalik about features that we wanted. I mean, we didn't even-- there are certain things about Ethereum that can't be changed. But there were things that-- there were things that could be changed. And there was this-- the design philosophy of most protocol builders has always been, hey, this protocol should be as simple as possible. And there's a lot of value in that principle. But our approach was the protocol should make it easy for developers to build apps that people can actually use. Whereas there's certain things about protocol design that make it impossible to create the kind of user experience we think normal people need no matter what you-- however education you give, and how to tutorials, and how important it is to secure your own keys, and all that stuff. So Flow is really about-- I mean, maybe to sort of simplify, you can think Flow is about reducing costs. And that's cost per transaction-- we're one of the cheapest of any scalable blockchain-- but also the carbon and environmental friendliness of the network as a whole. They're kind of related because basically, the cost you pay is for the networks and computers in the network to perform the tasks. And so because of how efficient the Flow architecture is, those are minimized while still being decentralized. So that's one aspect of it. And it's relatively straightforward. Because if you can transact and pay $0.50 in fees, if you have to pay $0.50 or $5 in fees, you're never going to do truly scalable, hey, free assets for everyone or things that are accessible to the everyday user who doesn't spend money every day in digital in every digital experience. So that's one thing, costs. And I think environmental friendliness is very important to newer generations as well. The second maybe richest kind of bucket of design differences or philosophical differences has been around safety, where because of the Flow programming language, because of the client wallet interface, because of simple decisions we made, the public-- you can keep the same public address on a Flow Wallet, but cycle the private keys in it so that you can-- so you don't have this, hey, my private key leaked. I have to get rid of-- basically, my wallet is forever useless. I have to cycle all the assets out, simple things like that that create a seamlessness on the application layer and the ability for the app not to feel like a complicated thing that you have-- the user has to assemble together. So there's a lot that goes into safety. The founder of Quantstamp said his-- their team did the deepest evaluation of our code and said it was by far the most secure blockchain they've ever-- the secure code they've ever reviewed just because of the perspective we've taken in terms of safety being so important in mainstream adoption. And every day, you hear about a Bored Ape hack and a Discord compromise leading to users losing their assets, et cetera. Every day you hear about people losing their private keys and this sort of thing. So safety was very, very important to us. And we can kind of get into a lot of the details there. And then the third thing is we wanted-- there's a lot of decisions in protocol design that have been carried over from Bitcoin to Ethereum, and then from Ethereum to other chains. And we wanted to be future-proof. So things like, the encryption curve that Flow uses is compatible with the secure enclave on iPhone and Android key store. Now we don't have a mobile wallet that uses it yet. And so it's not-- sort of hasn't broken through the mainstream yet. But it's-- we wanted to make sure that it has that future-proof capability. Flow Wallets are all smart contract wallets. They're fully programmable. Flow can be fully cross-chain. And so today, a company called LayerZero is working on an integration where you can use Flow Wallets to hold assets from any blockchain, Bitcoin, Ethereum, fungible, non-fungible. Doesn't matter. So the way it was written is as an application platform, not a token-- not a token machine. And so we think it's also extremely future-proof-- so cost, safety, and the concept of we've built it to be a mainstream consumer platform. And so things that haven't even been used yet, like true mobile-native compatibility, Flow has already sort of thought of. DAVID LAWEE: And so when you go and pitch IP holders that have some of the mainstream assets like a Disney, or kind of FIFA, or whoever are kind of the next partners, who are the competitors? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: At that level, they don't have the capability to build the products themselves. And so they're getting pitched by, I mean, some layer 1s that have spun up studio teams to build apps. Or they're getting pitched by app companies who have raised venture capital and said, hey, we can build these. But very few companies have anything in market that resembles anything that any of those brands would want to be associated with. And in terms of-- NBA Top Shot has on the order of millions of transactions in the last couple months, whereas if you look at something like a Bored Ape, very, very successful economy, but thousands, single-digit thousands, of transactions. So just a very different kind of scale-- familiarity with scale. So the competition doesn't necessarily-- look, when we talk to bigger brands, it's all about safety and all about the consumer experience. Part of that comes from dapper, which is 97% USD rather than crypto. You can buy $1-- an asset for $1, pay $0.05 in fees. It's sort of very streamlined. And you can imagine a user posting a link on Twitter and Instagram and people clicking through that link, buying that NFT without needing to know that it's an NFT. So a lot of it is that user experience layer that is a game-changer and is enabled because of Flow. But it isn't Flow directly. And then environmental friendliness, absolutely key. Because their superfans get up in arms if they think that the brand is doing something that is anti-environment. And that's something that, whether you're Disney, or EA, or whoever, you can't afford. And then it's-- and then it is things like, hey, it's future-proof, hey, it's-- you don't hear about NBA Top Shot accounts being hacked. You hear about Ethereum accounts being hacked all the time. So it's around consumer experience. DAVID LAWEE: And what's the pitch to crypto, to game companies, or designers working on products for crypto-native users? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Crypto-native-- so if by crypto-native you mean the average-- DAVID LAWEE: Like the next Axie type thing. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: So we historically have not had a strong pitch for fully kind of crypto-native folks, primarily because we're not-- Flow is so different than Ethereum. It's not EVM-compatible, Ethereum Virtual machine compatible. You need a centralized exchange to turn ETH into Flow. And so you need to do KYC. And so you don't have this pile of non-KYC money that needs places to sort of play. And so that drives a lot of payment volume in sort of non-custodial ecosystems. Because it's dollars that couldn't find a home inside-- that don't want to go inside bank accounts or anything else. They want stuff to do that is fully kind of outside the walls, so to speak. So that partially is getting-- I mean, that partially goes away once there are these layer 0 type trustless bridges and exchanges. So it could theoretically be-- it'll be inevitable that people will start all kinds of play to earn stuff once the permissionless is open. But a lot of the things currently on Flow are very kind of straightforward products that a user doesn't necessarily have to even know that it's cryptocurrency under the hood. They just know that this digital asset is tradable. This marketplace is transparent. Every transaction, I can go look it up from five years ago 10 years from now. The third-party developers seem to writing software for this product. And you know, today I have these two apps. Tomorrow I have another app. And it just kind of keeps-- the ecosystem keeps running. That's what the customer feels. They don't necessarily feel, oh, this is crypto, or blockchain, or whatever. That's sort of the ecosystem we've kind of attracted. And I think that that's good. Now what's the pitch going to be for the crypto-native developer tomorrow? It's going to be, well, we have the most users. We have 10 million accounts, most of which are real people. There isn't these speculative games to play. There aren't big decentralized exchanges on Flow that are giving out 20% annual yield, or monthly yield, or whatever. We don't have any of that stuff. Every person that has an account on Flow has it because they're using a product on Flow that they're paying for. And because of the, hey, Flow is different, Flow is-- a lot of the assets, US dollars, et cetera, there hasn't been this, hey, I bought a asset for $1. It turned into $100 in a day, or what happens on Ethereum, bought it for $2,000, sold it for $200,000. That hasn't been the thing that has attracted these customers. And I think that's a good thing, especially in this environment, where I think customer mentality is changing. It's no longer, hey, I have a pile of money I want to show off, or I'm just going to burn this cash, and oh, it turned into something new, and whatever. It's more about, hey, I'm a fan. How do I get more money-- value for my money. Because I've got $20 to spend on this ticket. And if I'm an NBA Top Shot collector, I actually get more for my money than if I'm not. Or if I'm a UFC Champions NFT holder, I get access to the Champions Club. I can go with my family. I can go with my friends and get them access to a open bar. That's the mentality that I think people will be attracted to in this new-- in this new world where everything's changed. For some people, they haven't realized it yet. But six months from now, 12 months from now, if the economy continues to get worse, people's mentality will be about-- just like it was 2008, right, when you had Airbnb, and Uber, and all these-- the passion economy was born out of a recession. This can be passion economy 2.0. By this, I mean sort of Web3 in general, but our products in particular as well. So that's kind of the mindset we're in is things have changed, but it's an opportunity more than anything. DAVID LAWEE: Awesome. And how do you think about the competition with other blockchains? One of the things that we've observed is just the amount of money that blockchains are handing out to developers. I know you've started-- you have been a participant, I guess, in the blockchain-- in the Flow Fund, $750 million Flow Fund. And how do you see that shaping behavior? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: So to clear, some numbers-- so we've invested in about 100 companies as Dapper Labs. We're very small amounts, usually from $25,000 to $100,000, some $1 million, more, but very small amounts. Those companies have gone on to raise over $3 billion from other venture capitalists, you know, Andreessen, COTU, Tiger, Sequoia, all of these folks. And the $750 million fund isn't our dollars. It's actually primarily from folks like Andreessen, and COTU, and USV, Venrock, CoinFund, whatever it might be. And so we've-- as Dapper Labs, we've seen all these folks splashing this money around. And we've seen, well, we have-- we've got cash in the bank. We could be splashing money. We could be selling tokens. But hey, I'd rather keep the tokens for the long term, and use the cash to build products that create more cash, and then get the VCs to invest in the next generation of products on top of our platforms. But we're going to get a transaction fee. We're going to get the sort of token appreciation value, et cetera. And that's the perspective we've taken is let professionals allocate capital to the best companies rather than have companies just come to us because we're handing out-- we're handing out cash and incentives. And so that's largely been the perspective we've taken with the capital. And the ecosystem is pretty well-funded, you know, $3.5 billion or so, mostly raised pretty recently. And that $750 million is over $1 billion now. Even now we're seeing VCs interested, at least in the early stage for sure. Because this is the only area in tech where there's 1,000x expansion opportunity in the TAM, right? Like, the TAM for project management software isn't going to get 1,000x bigger in the next year or two. But the number of people that have actually interacted with Web3 applications is tiny. And so there's-- and the number of NFT creators-- Andreessen was so proud to publish this report that said the dollar gain per NFT creator. And they sort of total dollars in the NFT economy divided by 22,000 creators. That's bonkers. 22,000 is-- you can't even-- you can't fill a big stadium with 22,000 people. And so that's how early all of this stuff is and how difficult-- the number of steps it takes to mint an NFT, and then the number of steps it takes for your community to buy that NFT. This is super early stage. We've just got to focus on how do we expand that thing by 1,000x, and everything else follows. Because there's-- monetization is kind of built into the rails here, which is also a little different than previous platform shifts. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, that's interesting. Yeah, let's talk a little bit about the recent trends in crypto, very recent trends. And one of the things that I found interesting was all the Bored Apes' celebrity purchases and then those quietly being removed from their profiles. Like, it just reflects the broader, I guess, concerns. And I would love to get your perspective on that. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Look, I mean, you've seen previous technology shifts, right? Like, there's-- it takes time for-- even something like open source software, for a decade plus, people were saying, well, is it a real thing, should you base your business on it, et cetera. Software as a service, right, is it a real thing? Could it-- would real businesses move towards it, whatever? That's like normal-- that's normal cycles. With crypto, the problem is you've got this supercharged nature of it, which is, with the token, everything has a market. Everything has a price. And so on the way up, there's this super-charged thing of everyone feeling like they're right. And on the way down, obviously everyone-- humans kind of get panicked and all this stuff. And so that-- Jesse Walden, who was at Andreessen at the time, called it tumorous growth. And I really-- it creates growth that is sort of like spike, crash, spike, crash, spike, crash. And you see it in Bitcoin over the last decade plus. And then you also see it in every crypto project still. Because people aren't-- two reasons-- I mean, developers and creators aren't good enough at managing it yet. I think we're getting better. And then second, I think consumers-- future generations get more and more comfortable with volatility. I almost think of it as generation-- the way that people were very uncomfortable with privacy in social media. But eventually now, people are posting pictures of their kids everywhere. People will get more comfortable with the price volatility. They'll understand some of the dynamics better. And that will mean less craziness on the way up because everyone's not FOMOing and less craziness on the way down because everyone's not panicking. People just realize that, hey, things cycle. And they sort of have markets built into them from day one because everything has a market. That's how I think behavior will evolve. But I think there's-- mostly, nothing's changed for me. And I think for our team, it's, hey owners, empathize with the customer and that their mentality has shifted. Netflix is down 75%, same as Bitcoin. There's no asset class that's been safe from any of this stuff. And so just build for value. Now there's a lot of noise out there, right, like things that-- and I won't count Bored Ape in that as noise. And we can debate the power in that brand and that community. But there's been a lot of noise where, obviously, that random picture of an animal isn't going to be worth $100,000. And when people realize that game of musical chairs unwinding, it can-- skeptics can feel very smart sort of pointing at it and saying, well hey, look, this technology wasn't ever going to work. But that's what it-- it was always a game of musical chairs. So like, it's fun until the music stops. But nobody-- you know what I'm saying? Like, the technology can be used for a lot of other things. And so I think that just is a natural cycle of things. I just encourage my team to keep their head down. Again, emphasize that, hey, the customer mindset has changed, but that this is a huge opportunity for our products. DAVID LAWEE: And what do you think the Googles, Amazons, and Microsofts of the world can do to help legitimize the space? Or are we even relevant? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: I think there's a fair amount that's super relevant. I mean, number one, we have a great partnership with Google Cloud. And that idea of powering the infrastructure is, I think, important. And whether that infrastructure is payments or hardware-- because our apps will need to run on your phones-- there's a lot to do there, right, like, both running the core blockchain network as well as recognizing that, hey, consumers are still going to need hardware devices to interact with these applications. And so how can the hardware be better suited for the new platform is, I think, maybe one layer of it. The next layer-- I don't know if there are open source efforts at Google. But just kind of contributing to these platforms and technologies seems like the best way to try and get exposure to it. And then the thing I get most excited about is creator platforms where, whether it's YouTube or others, this technology is about giving-- empowering creators to connect with their communities. Or at least the NFT component of it can be used there. And so how can Google or YouTube be a leader there rather than-- because at the end of the day, you guys are a technology company. And this is just another-- this is just another technology, in some ways, much easier than mobile to kind of adapt to because it's just about software, but in some ways harder. Because it's almost like social media. And of course, there's a little bit of history there with Google. But how do you change the thinking on what a customer-- what peer to peer interaction can look like? But I think just starting with, hey, the hardware component is something that no crypto-native company will start with, and then getting into the open source, and seeing ways to actually collaborate with these decentralized communities. So even Google can play an even bigger part in something like Flow that started as a Dapper Labs project but that could potentially-- that is now something that Fortune 500 and startups are building on top of, including some of your other bigger clients. So I think it can be a very fruitful ground. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, it seems like users-- like, we're talking about a tiny number of users right now, let's say-- your numbers of 10 million is actually what I thought the size of the whole market was in terms of people that have interacted with NFTs. So maybe it's-- the market size is 15 million right now or something in that zone. And I know that Andreessen-- in Andreessen's forecast, they were kind of trying to put some numbers to it and estimate the future-- see a billion users in 2031. So still quite a long time until we get to-- that was their-- you think sooner? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Way sooner. DAVID LAWEE: OK, that's interesting. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Way sooner, because you have-- the only problems are software and user experience. And the opportunity is so driven by-- there's value built in, right? If you think about the-- once we figure out how to make that growth non-tumorous, it can be-- and the phones are already there, right? How many Android phones already exist in people's pockets? DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, so your argument is they took the web growth and extrapolated from that. But now we're building on successive waves of technology that make it easier to drive adoption. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: That's how it always happens, right? Like, the speed of social media adoption, speed of everything, so much just kind of gets crunched. And I think social media is probably the closest analogy because it's also pure software and consumer behavior. DAVID LAWEE: So you feel like we're one successful game away from hundreds of millions of people interacting with these things? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Yeah, I mean, I think a 100 million-person game would be aggressive. But what happened with "CryptoKitties" was about 100k, NBA Top Shot, about a million. I think what we think about is, hey, how can NBA Top Shot go to 10 million? How can NFL All Day go to 10 million? And then, boom, how can you go to 20 million? And for us, it's a lot about integration where the fan is, whether it's real world, whether it's broadcast, streaming, et cetera, as well as-- we do think about gaming and gamification. But if you think about mobile apps, there's still 10 million, 20 million MA-- I mean, there's bigger ones, but the NBA, some of the NBA. So we think that this can go way beyond gaming in terms of number of users. Because it can be a lighter-weight adoption, it becomes part of their users' online profile. Like, we think of the NBA Top Shot collection as the user's profile page, more their Instagram home page than their Amazon order history, or however you want to think about it, or your "Fortnite" asset list, you know what I mean? Like, it's a little bit more who I am than what I have in a lot of ways. DAVID LAWEE: Awesome. I'm going to turn to some audience questions. So please send those in. The first one is, what is the role of UX in Web3? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: I think the role of UX in Web3-- I mean, the easy thing to say is to abstract everything out. But of course, that's not sufficient because then you don't maybe get the full value of it, et cetera. And so early custodial marketplace, centralized marketplaces is where [INAUDIBLE] like that. So I think of the value of Web3 is-- sorry, the role of user experience is keep the user safe while getting them the benefits of the technology. And that keep the user safe is, one, getting them to pay in the payment method that they have without having to jump through hoops that create lots of opportunities for failure, right? Like, sign up for a crypto account. Buy the crypto. Oh, I bought it at the wrong price, or you transferred it to the wrong wallet, or just infinite service area for problems. And then once you have the asset, keep it safe. And for different users, that's going to mean different things. We like the model that-- of saying the user needs to choose. Hey, you get a custodial account when you sign up. But then you can add-- you can go to your settings, add multifactor authentication, add your own password, take full custody and put it on your mobile phone. That's perfectly fine. That sort of full flow is nowhere close to-- I mean, even in our products, it's nowhere close to being fully there. And in the future, I think it's all about discovery and distribution, where, how do you even find what else I can do with my NFT or what other places I can take it into? How can I find what other communities I want to be a part of, what other assets are dropping, what things are being-- what opportunities are that for me maybe financially? No one's kind of-- there's no real distribution layer where-- the discovery layer is Twitter still, of how people find out what to do. So I think there's a lot of user experience from a how do I just use this thing, to how do I keep it safe, to how do I find the next thing, and connect with my friends, and all that fun stuff. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, so the vision you have is really one where the technology is abstracted away as opposed to people learning, necessarily, how this all works? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: The vision I have is one where people get the value up front, and they can peel back the layers and sort of look under the hood. And it's all there, right? It's not-- nothing is faked. But it's, up front, you just get the value. Because I think majority-- a majority of-- by the way, I should mention, the 10 million user number is user accounts. And so accounts can be created by different applications, the same thing on Ethereum, a little less so on Flow. Because there's less wallets and less people doing programmatic things. Like a user doesn't have 100,000 wallets like they might if they have a sort of bot that controls many, many accounts like they might on Ethereum. So the 10 million number isn't 10 million unique individuals. There's almost certainly some duplication there. But it is millions of individuals. Single-digit millions across the entire ecosystem would be-- so 10 million across the entire ecosystem would be a high estimate in my opinion-- DAVID LAWEE: OK. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: --of genuine people that have-- maybe even that tried it once, but at least have tried it. So I wanted to kind of touch on that. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, OK, thanks for clarifying that. It's actually hard to gauge these numbers. So this is really useful. We had that experience in our family of the onboarding challenge. We were all trying to play "Axie" over Thanksgiving last year. And my wife sent some Ethereum to Ronin Wallet. Boom, she lost $1,000. My son was so angry with her. It is-- it does feel like dial-up days of the internet, where you kind of had to-- oh, you have to do this, and then plug this in here, and figure it all out. And so that's why I was somewhat enticed by your vision of abstracting it away since that just seems a lot easier. But I wonder, who will do that? Will it be the game or application developers? Or will it be the Coinbases of the world that just onboard people for all of Web3? How do you imagine that playing out? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Well, I think it's going to be us. Because each individual game might onboard lots of users, but then they're going to need somewhere to-- OK, what's the next thing? Where do I put my stuff? How do I keep my stuff safe, all that stuff. And the Coinbases of the world are very centered around-- I mean, they started as financial companies first and foremost. And fundamentally, all of their-- I mean a lot of their NFT efforts have been kind of start-stop and not successful. But the biggest thing is they're-- I think they're not-- they're not smart contract first developers. And at the end of the day, the future-- like this-- every single wallet that we create is a programmable, composable LEGO piece among everything else. And so yes, create the user experience. Create the full flow. But then have it be open at the bottom so developers can then build that open ecosystem so it's not Minitel, to our conversation before this. It doesn't end up being just the user experience that gives the user the answer once. But it also lets new stuff enter at the bottom, and be fully composable, fully open, fully decentralized. And I think that innovation is not done at the protocol level either, where there's things that are left in terms of making Flow fully mobile-native, showing the world how that even works, making a real cross-chain ecosystem. The vision I have is developers will choose blockchains based on-- hey, I'm going to do my computation on Flow. I'm going to take payment from Ethereum, and Bitcoin, and Flow, and Solana, and whatever else. I might do my decentralized exchange work on this other sidechain. I might use Compound for-- which is going to have its own chain-- for lending and borrowing to balance my books, or whatever it might be. Just like today, a developer says, I'm going to use Google Cloud for this, and I'm going to use Redis for that, and I'm going to use whatever it might be. Everything has its own sort of what it's good for. Now we think that we've built the application, computation layer. And then what the user will-- the user interface layer into what all of these other assets, and chains, and stuff will be. But it will be the developer that chooses, hey, how do I assemble this stuff together? And the consumer says, ooh, pretty picture, I want that. Or hey, I want to engage with my friend in this way. Or hey, I'm invited to a challenge, or whatever it might be. It's not going to be anything about the technology. I mean, just the last thing I'll say is the customer doesn't think-- I mean, you guys know this better than anyone. They don't think to themselves, which search engine am I going to use? Oh Google, cool, cool, cool. And they don't switch unless it's bad. Or, oh, which ridesharing app? And I have a network of-- I'm going to compare ridesharing apps. Just use-- the product becomes the category in a way. The customer doesn't sit there choosing what wallet they want to use on what chain to buy what asset. It just needs to be much more seamless. And I think-- and I think it's going to take someone that's going to dogfood their own product as well. So I think it's going to be-- it's going to be us. And it's going to be pretty soon. Now how quickly that goes to a billion users will, I think, be where maybe my estimates are more aggressive than most. DAVID LAWEE: Yeah, they are. What is the-- one of the nice things about building everything on Flow is you have a little bit more control over the security of the ecosystem. And when you start talking about bridges or unifying chains, you kind of lose some of that. When do you feel like that will kind of be minimized so that people can be comfortable moving things across chains? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: So it's already-- so Dapper Labs has stepped back from that stuff quite a while ago, maybe six or nine months ago. And since that, there have been multiple auditors that have been pushing-- they've been doing light security review, but they've been pushing other people's apps live. And there's now been a process of three, four months of hardening, and testing, and audits, and things like that to make sure it's now ready to be completely open. And I think the next 15 days or so is what I believe it's slated to be. And it's in testing now. And the reason for that is-- I don't know how much this group has looked into programming languages on blockchains, but there's this concept of resource-oriented programming, where the programming language itself sort of respects rules around digital assets, and ownership, and also governance. So the programming language itself is sort of mapped to-- it says, hey, if I own this asset, it won't let a command from you to move it even sort of compile. Because it sort of recognizes, hey, I own this asset. Whereas in every other programming language, an ownership is very much just a sort of hacked together thing. Because the digital things aren't unique, right? They're just-- everything's a data structure. And so that's the primary thing that makes Flow-- and Libra was the-- we started working on this research-oriented concept in parallel with the Libra team. They published the Libra whitepaper first. And so we-- they called it resources. And we sort of adapted our work to them. We've been-- then we worked with that team to make sure our programming language is compatible with the one they came up with. I mean, now, obviously, it's not going to ship in that shape. But that concept of resource-oriented programming makes it much safer for-- because you're unsaved smart contract can't access my assets unless it compromises my wallet as well. And Flow has things like human-readable security, where the wallet will be able to tell the user what they're signing. On MetaMask, or in general on Ethereum, it's not possible. The wallet doesn't know. It's just this gibberish sort of string of whatever it is. And even to the extent that you might have an NFT-- and the other thing is you can't just airdrop NFTs into Flow Wallets. A user has to accept that airdrop. Whereas today, on Ethereum, you have exploits where I can airdrop an NFT that looks exactly like your NFT. You'll go look at it in OpenSea. You'll say, oh, I have two of these things. I'm going to list one of them for sale. Just by listing it for sale, that can compromise your account. Because that can give the-- if it's a malicious smart contract, can give full access to your wallet contents. And that's just bonkers. There's no way that that, by itself, is going to be able to succeed. Because anything that's that unsafe doesn't go true mainstream. And the other example is smartphones before the App Store, where it was unsafe to install anything. You had to make sure, hey, the version number is compatible with the patch that you had on your operating system. Otherwise you're going to get a blue screen of death on your Windows CE, whatever it was. And that just made it so that only pro users installed stuff. And so there was less developers developing because there was less users installing. And that concept of safety is just really important for mainstream adoption. DAVID LAWEE: And do you think that's going to be easier to do in a kind of more controlled environment like Flow versus something like Solana where you maybe have more, I don't know, independent developer momentum? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Well, again, I think that the control is not an area where Flow is going to-- Flow is already open and decentralized. And it's going to be completely permissionless very shortly. And so it's a little bit more of the actual core design of it that keeps the safety rather than, hey, there's just less stuff on it. I think the less stuff on it, my fear is that it's a little bit intranet versus internet, or AOL versus open web, or Minitel versus internet. But what we do is we have that wallet layer on top. And we say, hey look, anything within the wallet layer, we keep you safe. It's almost like guaranteed, essentially, that you can't have your stuff hacked. You can't have your stuff stolen. We keep all your-- every application that you use is reviewed. No one's going to hack your stuff. Outside of that wallet ecosystem, it's almost-- in my mind, it's almost like incognito mode on a browser, where it's a little bit less safe. I mean, that's not what incognito mode is. But in a sense, we create a little sandbox that says, hey, in this sandbox, you're in the Wild West. Or there's sort of things that happen that-- again, because of Flow, it can't compromise your whole thing. But it can-- there's all kinds of stuff that hasn't even been thought of yet. So that's a little bit of-- Flow is an open system. But it's built in a way where applications can preserve customer experience. And Dapper is the best way we preserve customer experience for most newbies. DAVID LAWEE: Now if you look at it, there's been kind of, let's say, 150 million or so people who own Bitcoin in the world, some number of people who own Ethereum that's kind of significantly less, and then kind of 10 million people transacting. We're at the-- kind of probably an inflection point for regulation. What are your-- and I guess you were early in terms of soliciting those views. What's your kind of prediction in terms of what happens in the next year? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: I mean, I'm wary of making predictions on areas I'm not an expert in. I'm definitely not an expert in regulators. As Dapper Labs, our head of regulatory affairs is ex-SEC, ex-CFTC. Our head of government affairs is Alison Cutler. She's also fantastic. So we do stay close to both regulators as well as international governments. You know, UK, Spain, they're doing a lot of things in gaming. And they're considering NFTs. US has been very friendly so far-- or US, Canada, I should say-- friendly towards NFTs. Obviously, a lot of concern around assets that have royalties built in or sort of profit sharing from a securities perspective. But almost everything else seems to fall cleanly into sort of, hey, it's a trading card, hey, it's a commodity, that sort of thing. And I think there hasn't been enough widespread scams, and hacks, and things where consumer protection is going to get-- most of the people that get scammed and hacked are people like us who are technologists that just make silly mistakes. And it happens-- it happens way more often than people admit. And so-- I'm saying that on behalf of a friend. And so the-- and so that's sort of the-- I guess at least what I see from my seat, which is there's folks that-- countries in particular that have a specific focus on gaming, that are looking at NFTs. And we want to make sure our voice is heard. And so we have active efforts in speaking with lawmakers and others, trying to explain to them, hey look, in a game environment, that digital asset-- not transparent, not tradable. Here, there are certain rules that the game maker even is, in a sense, not in control of. And so it's better for the customer in almost every way. And that's just a conversation we need to have sometimes one on one. DAVID LAWEE: So when you think about when you're talking to partners for, let's say, music NFTs where the securities laws may be kind of harder to determine, how are you navigating that? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Good question. We don't do anything directly in music as Dapper Labs. So we have a number of expert contacts in our network. And we're close with Jason-- Justin Blough at Royal. And we look at their work. We've got a number of music platforms on Flow, like Record Shop and others. We have folks like Steve Stout as our lead backer. So we're not the music experts. We tend to put folks in touch with others. On the long tail, there's a lot of willingness to experiment, on the high end, not a lot of willingness to go into the gray area. We understand that. But I think in terms of the high end, the world's top community owners, there's so much-- there are many ways they can engage their community that doesn't involve direct revenue sharing and profit sharing. And that's what we tend to focus on is kind of net new-- DAVID LAWEE: More the experience NFTs. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Experience NFTs, new kinds of engagement, types of engagement that's not currently monetized. I mean, even like going backstage, even when the artist isn't there, and sort of being able to experience a piece of the show, and kind of creating a metagame game around being a Lady Gaga fan, being a Chainsmokers fan, whatever it might be, and rewarding their top fans with other things in the future, potentially experiential, potentially physical, potentially digital. It doesn't have to be dollars. And in fact, maybe it doesn't-- maybe shouldn't be. DAVID LAWEE: So in the short term, I'd imagine there's going to be some kind of regulation around stablecoins and kind of protecting the economy to the extent that it's at risk around the DeFi infrastructure and less around the kind of what an NFT can be, can't be, since that gets into really edge use cases that are pretty small. And so do you imagine kind of playing it up the middle in a sense, like being relatively conservative in terms of how expansive the NFT that you involve yourself is going to be? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: As Dapper Labs, yes. But because of the permissionless nature of Flow, anyone will be able to do anything. We can see what works. Things like Audius are pretty interesting on other platforms. And they're looking for new homes given the downtime issues and reliability of Solana. So there's all kinds of opportunity for Flow as a platform. And we, as app developers, we're going to watch and see. Personally, I believe that experimentation is good, and it leads to new customer value. And so regulation shouldn't inhibit it. But as a company, we always want to be on the right side of-- right side of the law. DAVID LAWEE: And do you think that's going to slow things down? One of the questions is, when will we see titles for homes being on NFTs? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: So titles for homes was actually one of the first drivers of the NFT standard. And obviously, as you might imagine, it's incredibly complex and globally complex, I think. So I don't know. I think if you track the history of the internet, it took a while until people were-- it took until almost everyone had access until things like real utilities became-- that people started relying on the internet for real utilities and sort of life and death stuff. And in a sense, I think that real estate in particular, given the regulatory environment, et cetera, might not be one of the first things to be fully tokenized. But I think almost everything else-- there's going to be so many things that are-- I said this recently at one of these conferences, which was, just like every piece of information that mattered to everyone else, anyone else is online. I think every piece of-- every asset and piece of value that mattered-- that could matter to anyone else will be on chain. And it'll just have access to global markets, global derivatives, global-- it'll be part of everybody's portfolio. But that will take quite some time. DAVID LAWEE: I guess my last question-- and there are a lot of Googlers who are kind of contemplating how to think about whether to jump in now. What's your advice to people? ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Yeah, jump in now. I mean, I'm sure there's opportunities within Google to get engaged. But like I said, there's so much open source opportunity. There are so many companies working on interesting projects, including Dapper Labs. And companies in Web3, including Dapper Labs, are also growing and hiring aggressively. Now I think that the biggest thing I'd love to see is anyone who's involved with creators to just ask them about, hey look, what ways would you like to engage with your community? And creators include game developers. And there are so many that, hey, oh no, I wouldn't do crypto. But I really want tradable digital assets. It's like, well, great., that's something that is totally possible-- or more efficient payments, or larger payments, or whatever it might be. So there's just incredible opportunities. I would encourage folks to think of it as a technology, not necessarily as-- in the silos that already exist today, like speculative marketplaces and whatever it might be. DAVID LAWEE: Thank you so, Roham. This has been such a pleasure. It's really just a privilege to have the opportunity to talk to you. ROHAM GHAREGOZLOU: Absolutely. Thank you, David, a lot of fun. [MUSIC PLAYING]
